title: Breaching a role-specific requirement carries the same default culpability as breaching a general one
content:
A.1.5.6 layers two rule sets on every Alignment Conserver: the general AC requirements in Article A.1.5, plus role-specific requirements for Aligned Delegates (A.1.6) or Facilitators (A.1.7). It states that "breaching these role-specific requirements and responsibilities is misalignment equivalent to breaching the general AC-requirements."

The Action Tenet at A.1.5.6.0.4.1 turns the equivalence into an instruction with a carefully placed limit: "Facilitators must not default to assigning greater or lesser culpability on the sole basis of whether the breached rule is role-specific or general. Apart from this caveat, misaligned acts can have varying degrees of severity or harm, and should be individually evaluated by the Facilitator in any action."

What is being prohibited is a **heuristic**, not judgment itself. The natural intuition — general rules are foundational, so breaching them is worse; or conversely, role-specific rules are technicalities — is exactly the shortcut that lets an adjudicator arrive at a preferred severity without arguing about the facts. Removing the heuristic forces severity to be justified on impact.

The underlying design point is that the general/specific split is an artefact of *document organization*, not of importance. Whether a requirement landed in the shared Article or in the role's own Article reflects how many roles it applies to, nothing more. Letting a filing decision drive culpability would make the tree's structure a hidden sentencing table.

This is the same instinct as the formal-occupancy rule read from the other side: there, a formal fact is made dispositive because substance is unprovable; here, a formal fact is made irrelevant because substance is available. The Atlas is consistently trying to keep adjudication anchored to whichever of the two is actually checkable.
description: A.1.5.6.0.4.1 bars facilitators from grading severity by whether the rule was general or role-specific, while still requiring case-by-case evaluation of actual harm.
